posts.title: My first week with React: from confused to obsessed
posts.content: I started this job three weeks ago knowing barely any React, and honestly the first two days were just me staring at JSX wondering why HTML and JavaScript were on a first-name basis. Then I built my first component that actually re-rendered when I clicked a button and I did a small fist pump at my desk. Props still trip me up sometimes but I'm getting there, one console.log at a time.

posts.title: Key prop mistakes that will haunt your console
posts.content:
Using the array index as a key felt harmless until items started reordering and our list animations turned into chaos. Lesson learned the hard way.

```jsx
{items.map((item) => (
  <ListItem key={item.id} data={item} />
))}
```

Use something stable and unique, not the index, not Math.random(), and definitely not the item's name if two items can share one. React's diffing algorithm is only as good as the keys you give it.

posts.title: Why I still get excited about closures after 10 years
posts.content: I know closures are JavaScript 101, but every time I explain one to a junior on the team and watch it click for them, I get a little rush. A function remembering the variables from where it was created, even after that outer function has finished running, still feels a bit like magic even though I understand exactly why it works. Ten years in and I have not gotten bored of this language yet.

posts.title: Optional chaining saved my Friday afternoon
posts.content:
Somewhere deep in a nested API response, one field was occasionally missing, and our app was throwing 'cannot read property of undefined' at the worst possible times.

```js
const city = user?.address?.city ?? 'Unknown';
```

One line, no more defensive if-chains, no more crashes. I added this everywhere touching that API response and went home on time for once.

posts.title: Flexbox vs Grid: an unnecessary rivalry
posts.content: People argue about this like you have to pick a side forever. I use Flexbox for one-dimensional layouts, like a row of buttons or a navbar, and Grid the second I'm arranging things in both rows and columns. They're not rivals, they're just tools for different shaped problems, and most real layouts end up using both at once anyway.

posts.title: The commit message that haunts me to this day
posts.content: Early in my career I pushed a commit with the message 'fix' to a shared branch, right before a demo, with zero context about what was actually fixed. My tech lead still brings it up in retrospectives, years later, as the platonic ideal of what not to do. These days I write commit messages assuming a stranger will read them at 2am trying to figure out why production is on fire, because eventually, that stranger is me.
posts.author: raj_builds

posts.title: A .gitignore snippet that saved me from committing node_modules again
posts.content:
I have, on more than one occasion, committed node_modules to a repo and made everyone's pull request diff unreadable. Here's the bare minimum I now paste into every new project before writing a single line of code.

```text
node_modules/
.env
dist/
.DS_Store
*.log
```

Five lines, saved me an equal number of apologies in team chat.
posts.author: jess_codes

posts.title: GitHub Actions workflow for running tests on every PR
posts.content:
We kept merging PRs that quietly broke the test suite because nobody ran it locally before merging. This workflow fixed that for us in about fifteen minutes.

```yaml
name: CI
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
```

Now a red X shows up right on the PR if something's broken, and nobody can pretend they didn't see it.
posts.author: senior_sam

posts.title: My favorite git aliases after years of typos
posts.content:
I misspell 'checkout' at least once a day, so eventually I gave in and set up aliases for the commands I run constantly.

```bash
git config --global alias.co checkout
git config --global alias.st status
git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --all"
```

`git lg` in particular has replaced at least three different GUI tools I used to rely on just to understand a messy branch history.

posts.title: Confession: I still have a soft spot for jQuery
posts.content: I know, I know. But there was something genuinely satisfying about $(this).fadeOut() just working, no build step, no bundler config, no hooks to think about. It's not what I reach for in a modern React app, but for a quick static page or a tiny widget, I still sometimes default to it out of pure muscle memory, and I'm not embarrassed about it anymore.
